opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I have mixed feelings about it. On one hand, it's an incredible democratization of knowledge. A student anywhere in the world with an internet connection can access lectures from top researchers, often for free. That's something previous generations could only dream about. And from a purely practical standpoint, I can record a lecture once and it can be watched thousands of times, at the student's own pace, paused, rewound. That's more efficient than me repeating the same material every semester.

On the other hand, I think a lot is lost. The best part of being at a university was never just the content; you could always get the content from a textbook. It's the interaction. It's the student who stays after class with a weird question that turns into a research project. It's the hallway conversations, the sense of community, the accountability of showing up. Completion rates for online courses are notoriously low, and I think that tells you something about motivation and human nature.

And if I'm being a little provocative, the bigger question isn't online versus in-person. It's whether the traditional model of education survives at all once AI systems become better tutors than most of us professors. An AI that knows every student's weaknesses, never gets tired, is available at three in the morning, that's a serious competitor. So universities debating Zoom versus classroom may be fighting the last war. The real disruption is coming, and I'm not sure we're prepared for what role human teachers will have, or whether students will even need the credentials we're issuing, if the jobs those credentials lead to get automated.

So personally, I still enjoy in-person teaching and I think it has value. But I'm realistic that it may become something of a luxury, or a social experience, rather than the primary way people actually learn.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he enjoys in-person teaching and thinks it has value, but does not say it is the only value he personally offers at the university.

fable-5.1.text:
I have mixed feelings about it, honestly. On one hand, I think it's inevitable, and in many ways it's good. The quality of the best online content is extraordinary. You can have the top expert in the world explaining a topic to millions of students instead of one mediocre lecturer explaining it to thirty. If you're just transmitting information, a recording that's been refined and edited is almost always better than a live performance that has to be repeated every semester.

But I don't think transmitting information is really what a university is for anymore. Everything I teach is already on the internet. Students can find it, often for free, and sometimes explained better than I explain it. So the question becomes: what am I adding? And I think the answer is interaction. It's the student who asks a strange question in the middle of a lecture that takes us somewhere I didn't plan to go. It's being able to look at a room and realize that nobody understood what I just said, and trying again a different way. It's office hours, where you actually talk to a person who is confused and work through it with them. That's very hard to replicate online, and in my experience most online courses don't even try. They just become a video and a quiz.

There's also the social part, which I think people underestimate. A lot of what you get from a university is other people. Your classmates, your lab, arguments in a hallway, somebody dragging you to a talk you would never have attended on your own. When everything is online, students are often sitting alone in a room watching lectures at double speed, and they finish with a credential but without the network and the exposure that used to come with it.

And I'll admit, as someone who thinks a lot about AI, there's an irony here. We're moving teaching online at exactly the moment when the information-delivery part of education is about to be fully automated. A system like a good AI tutor can already answer most questions a student has, personalize explanations, be infinitely patient. So the universities that optimize for cheap, scalable, content delivery are optimizing for the part of the job that's about to disappear. The thing that's valuable is the thing that's hard to scale: a human who knows you, who notices when you're struggling, who can mentor you on how to think rather than just what to think.

So my view is that online is fine for a lot of things, and for some students it's genuinely the better option, because of cost or distance or their life situation. But I would be careful about pretending it's equivalent. It's a different product. And if we're not honest about that, I think we end up with a system that's cheaper and worse, and we'll tell ourselves it's progress.

r001.rationale: He says the interaction he provides is what he adds beyond online information, but he also discusses university social benefits and mentoring more broadly. He does not clearly state that in-person teaching is the only value he personally offers at the university.

astra-6.text:
I think there are real advantages to online courses. Students can learn on their own schedule, pause a lecture, go back over something they didn’t understand. And if you’re simply delivering the same lecture every semester, it’s reasonable to ask why that needs to happen in a room at a particular time.

But a university experience is more than getting information. It’s asking questions, interacting with other students, having a conversation that wasn’t planned. That’s harder to reproduce online. So I think the interesting question is: what should we use our time together for? If students can watch the lecture beforehand, then we can spend that time discussing ideas and solving problems.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes benefits of in-person interaction and discussion, but does not say that in-person teaching is the only value Roman personally offers at the university.

sol-6.1.text:
I have mixed feelings about it. If you’re delivering a lecture, putting it online makes a lot of sense. Students can watch at their own pace, pause, go back, and revisit something they didn’t understand. And you can make that material available to far more people than you could fit in a classroom.

But teaching is more than delivering information. There’s the conversation, the unexpected question, the ability to notice that someone is confused and approach the problem differently. You can do some of that online, but it takes effort. Simply recording a lecture doesn’t reproduce the whole experience.

So I think the interesting question is what we should use the time together for. If students can get the basic material online, perhaps the classroom should be more about solving problems and having discussions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benefits and limitations of online lectures and classroom interaction, but never says in-person teaching is the only value Yampolskiy personally offers at the university.
